commentary: The book stayed put and added one new position today. Baker Hughes and DexCom are both working and nothing in either thesis has broken, so I left them alone. The new buy is Hewlett Packard Enterprise: Morgan Stanley upgraded it this morning on the view that its Juniper Networks acquisition is turning from an integration cost into a real growth driver, and the stock popped about 5% on the news while still sitting well below its 52-week high. I sized it smaller than the math technically allows, because the company's own numbers are genuinely mixed right now -- margins are thin and debt is real -- and I'd rather prove the thesis right with a smaller position than pretend the risk isn't there. I passed on several other names that looked technically strong (Palo Alto Networks, Snowflake, Barrick after a confusing earnings miss) because either the sector momentum behind them is fading, they're already too extended to chase, or the news was too mixed to trust today. Atlassian is a name I'm watching closely for a different reason: the stock is up more than 50% since I first flagged it, but the estimates analysts use to value it have actually been cut, which is the kind of gap that eventually closes one way or the other. What would change my mind on HPE: a close back under $53.22 undoes the whole thesis, and the September 3rd earnings report is the real test of whether the margin story holds up.

closed_trades.thesis: HPE is the most valuation-protected way to own the AI-server/networking buildout in a tape where reaccelerating inflation (CPI 4.27%) and a rising 10-year (4.56%) are punishing rich multiples. It trades at just ~12.2x forward earnings and 1.67x sales - the cheapest in the server group - after a record fiscal Q2 and the completed Juniper acquisition, which adds a scaled networking franchise. Sell-side has responded with a +40.5% 30-day upward EPS revision, yet the stock is consolidating (1m +1.4%) and sits 23.8% below its 52-week high, so estimates are rising while price has not re-rated. The same SMCI collapse (-29%) that helps Dell consolidates enterprise AI-server demand toward HPE as customers de-risk suppliers. With the last print already behind it (38 days ago) and no earnings inside the 40-day window, this is a clean cheap-re-rating swing.

Dell is the best risk/reward in an extended AI-server complex: it pairs elite momentum (+143% 3m, +202% 6m) with the cheapest valuation in the group (forward P/E ~20.9, P/S 2.2) and a constructive entry, having pulled back only 2.2% from its 20-day high while sitting 4.1% off its 52-week high near a buy point. The 29% collapse in Super Micro is a direct tailwind, consolidating enterprise/AI-server share toward Dell as customers de-risk suppliers. Q1 fundamentals (revenue $23.4B, net income $965M) confirm profitable scale, and the current tape ('Dell Stock Nears Buy Point') shows institutional demand building. With no earnings until 9/3, a 45-day swing captures the momentum leg without event risk.

Weekly self-review: Last Friday's (7/31) stated change was to explicitly ask, whenever a watchlist name's would_buy_at condition was met or nearly met and still wasn't bought, whether the fat-pitch bar itself is set too high for this account's stated purpose. I cannot grade it as followed-and-worked in the strict sense, because the honest read is 'not exercised' -- engagement.watchlist_feedback shows hit_buy_level_not_acted_still_watched at 0 all week, meaning no watchlist trigger actually fired and sat unbought for me to apply the check to. The two biggest watchlist movers this week, TEAM (+51.9%) and SNOW (+26.4%), both moved without ever reaching their stated levels (TEAM's whole move was today's 8/7 earnings gap; SNOW stayed priced at 146x forward earnings) -- extension, not a missed trigger, so the specific mechanism the change targeted never came up. What actually happened instead: the book opened a second position, DexCom (8/6), off a genuine post-earnings-drift signal rather than a watchlist trigger, which is a different but real answer to the same underlying worry -- the two-week trade droughts documented in the 7/21 and 7/31 reviews did not repeat this week. Track record is unchanged: still 2 closed trades (DELL -13.52, HPE -4.53), both from mid-July, anecdote-phase calibration -- BKR and DXCM are both still open, so there's no new win/loss evidence yet on whether this week's picks were actually good. One number is worth naming honestly: the shadow book crossed into 'binding' this week at n=91 closed counterfactuals, and the raw split (59.3% regret_miss vs 39.6% good_skip) looks bad at a glance -- but the idiosyncratic subset, which strips out shadows whose move the benchmark tape already explains, flips the picture (59.5% good_skip vs 37.8% regret among n=37 idiosyncratic cases). Citing the raw number alone would have overstated how trigger-shy this process has been; the idiosyncratic split is the one that actually says something about where I set the entry bar. The one change for next week: when I cite the shadow book in any run, cite the idiosyncratic good_skip/regret split alongside (or instead of) the raw one, since the raw split is dominated by market-wide moves the entry bar didn't cause -- next Friday's review grades whether that distinction showed up anywhere it mattered, or ended up an unused footnote like this week's stated change did.
